prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, bringing the measurement of frequency and time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B040 as a stand-alone prize to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Having read the full round-1 exchange, the chair's first question is the one I should answer plainly. The distinct invention is this: the magic-wavelength lattice makes the trap's light shift cancel on the clock transition, so that thousands of neutral atoms, held tightly enough to be free of Doppler and recoil shifts, can be interrogated at once. That is what the comb (a counter for optical frequencies, 2005) and single-ion clocks (one absorber, 2012) do not contain. It converts clock stability into a statistics-and-coherence problem with many atoms, which is why lattice clocks reached 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and why Ye's Fermi-degenerate and many-body clocks exist at all. Is it discovery or instrument? It is an invention verified by experiment, and the verification is the part I weigh most: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, NPL) have reproduced and surpassed each other, intercompared across fibre links, and the instrument has then been used for physics, with millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter searches. Draft wording for the citation, as the chair asked: 'for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, bringing the measurement of frequency and time to the 10^-18 level'. On credit, Katori proposed the magic-wavelength scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group carried it to record accuracy and stability and developed the many-body clock. This is a split by contribution type, which I can defend. Six of eight members now carry B040 in their preferred configuration, but several arrived after reading each other, so I rest my own position on the evidence above and not on that count.
statement.case_against: The reservations I take most seriously, after round 1, are three. First, the credit boundary: Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Lemonde, Gill and Takamoto did work that is part of why the clocks reached their present performance, and none of us has seen the external expert reports on early Tokyo versus JILA priority. Two names are defensible but not beyond dispute, and I would not add a third: any third name would be a judgement call on a group effort, and the weaker the justification, the more it harms the clean Katori-Ye split. Second, the precedent argument made by Mehlig and Eriksson: a third prize in precision measurement in twenty years can look like a preference of the committee for one kind of physics. I think the science answers it, but the committee should not pretend the concern is empty. Third, the pending redefinition of the second shows the community's confidence, but a skeptic can still call the headline application prospective. I regard that as procedural and not as evidence that the physics is unproven, because the intercomparisons already exist.

responses.point: Danielsson moved toward B040 but prefers a two-part prize with B028 (Hosono, iron-based superconductors), and asks whether the lattice clock citation can be worded so it is not just a second metrology prize.
responses.response: I am glad he has moved, and the wording above is my answer on the citation: it rests on the many-atom magic-wavelength interrogation, not on 'a better clock'. On pairing with B028 I do not agree, though not because I doubt Hosono's experiment. He himself calls the pairing a combination with no common thread, which a purist would call a compromise, and I would add that adding a part that nobody except Danielsson and Olsson prefers dilutes a two-name case that is already clean. The unexplained pairing mechanism and the fast Tc increases by other groups also leave the citation wording for B028 delicate (family of materials, Kamihara, no implied record). I would not stand in the way of B028 as a separate decision in a later year, but I would rather the committee defend one achievement fully than two with a compromise between them. I understand that this leaves my position here in minority within the B040 group, and I will accept that.

responses.point: Mehlig treats B040 as the better-attributed fallback to B061 but worries that it is a third prize for better clocks after 2005 and 2012, and that the broad support alone does not settle it.
responses.response: I agree that support counts do not settle it, and I do not offer them as a reason. My reason is that the three prizes are about different things: frequency counting (comb), control of one quantum system (ions), and a many-atom interrogation scheme with a cancelled light shift (lattice). Ion clocks reached comparable accuracy, but not comparable stability, because they interrogate a single absorber. The lattice clock is where optical frequency standards became a many-body measurement problem, and that is a reasoned claim about novelty and not a taste for clocks. I welcome his statement that B040 is acceptable if attribution is the deciding factor, since for me it is. Where I still differ from him is that I would keep B061 as an alternative only: until the committee can state how Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are handled, a three-name allocation to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the weaker one on credit.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that B061 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) is a conceptual surprise confirmed by experiment, that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap can be handled by citation wording, and he ranked B040 last at opening, deferring to atomic physicists.
responses.response: I take his point that B061 is a conceptual shift and that the prediction, the HgTe observation and two decades of confirmation are exactly the chain I respect. His round-1 answer on B017 was fair: I accept that crowded 1991 priority is at least as bad a credit problem as the BHZ gap, and I have dropped B017 as a first choice for that reason. But I do not think a citation can repair the BHZ gap. If the citation says 'prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation in HgTe', it names the HgTe proposal as part of the credit and then omits its authors, which is hard to defend before external reviewers. A citation that avoids it would have to be so generic that it loses the experiment. For B040 the corresponding gap is smaller and sits at the margin, not in the middle of the chain. I would ask him what he would need to see for the final ballot: a scientific objection to the lattice clock, or only distance from the field?

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B040 first and shares the view that the 2005 and 2012 prizes concern frequency measurement and single-ion control, and she asked for a colleague outside AMO to test the case.
responses.response: We agree on the pair and on the distinction. I would add one shared caution: neither of us should be the only judge of whether this reads as a fundamental result, and we are both inside this community, so the tests from Johansson, Danielsson, Mehlig and Eriksson are useful to me, not an obstacle. I also accept her argument on B017, so the two of us no longer have a credible second part. I will keep B017 only as an alternative ballot.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, accepts two names provisionally but asks whether the Katori-to-Ye allocation is truly decisive or whether Ludlow, Hinkley or Bloom did work of the same weight, and says he would not defend a third.
responses.response: I would not defend a third either. My assessment is that Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's accuracy and many-body clocks, are the identifiable origins of the two programmes, while Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom were decisive members of Ye's group's work, and Lemonde and Gill led parallel efforts elsewhere. Group members who did the apparatus work are normally credited through the group leader, and that is the usual boundary the prize has drawn. I cannot settle early priority between Tokyo and JILA from what I have in front of me, and I would want the external expert reports to confirm it before the final ballot. If they showed a third person with a claim equal to Katori and Ye, I would revisit the configuration, but I do not expect that.

responses.point: Olsson combined B040 with B028 (Hosono) as two separate achievements with clean attribution, setting aside her own first choice B046.
responses.response: I respect her reasoning that both parts are mature and cleanly credited, and I agree about Hosono's discovery being an unexpected experimental result. My objection is again not to the experiment but to the construction: if a part is added to widen a prize and not because the committee believes it is among the best achievements of the year, the choice of part tends to follow what is available. Her own reservation about the unexplained mechanism points the same way. For that reason I prefer the stand-alone B040 and would regard B028 as a candidate for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the external expert reports confirm that Katori (concept and first lattice clock) and Ye (accuracy and many-body clocks) are the decisive credits, with no third person of comparable weight; I cannot verify early Tokyo and JILA priority myself.

Whether the committee will read the 2005 and 2012 prizes as making a lattice clock prize incremental, which is the main objection from Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson, and which I answer on scientific grounds but cannot dismiss as irrelevant.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as confirmation or as a reason to wait; I regard it as procedural but I am an interested party on the side of metrology.
Whether a stand-alone B040 will be seen by the condensed-matter members as too narrow a prize, and whether B028 or B061 would be the better second part in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I spent part of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder; Hall shared the 2005 prize and Jun Ye is a JILA colleague of that lab's tradition, but I have no collaboration or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. I lead part of WACQT, which is Chalmers-led and relevant to B055 but not to B040. The chair's summary flagged the Hall connection and I think the committee should weigh my B040 advocacy with it in mind; I have no financial or institutional interest in the outcome.
